claims.claim: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is an authentication system that requires more than one distinct type of authentication factor for successful authentication, per NIST SP 800-63B rev. 4; Microsoft's identity documentation lists MFA methods such as push notifications, SMS sign-in, OATH tokens, and security keys as usable for secondary authentication.

Authentication proof comes in three factor categories: something you know, something you have, and something you are; MFA must combine different categories, so two proofs from the same category (e.g., password plus PIN) still count as one factor, and NIST's AAL2 requires proof of possession and control of two distinct authentication factors.

The core benefit of MFA is that a compromised password alone is not enough to sign in; CISA reports, based on industry research, that users who enable MFA are up to 99 percent less likely to have an account compromised, and CISA calls MFA one of the most important cybersecurity practices for reducing the risk of intrusions.

Common MFA methods are instances of the factors: one-time codes sent by SMS or generated by an authenticator app (something you have), push approvals sent to an app, security keys such as FIDO2 keys and passkeys (something you have, cryptographic possession), and biometrics such as fingerprint or face (something you are); Microsoft documents these methods in its authentication-methods table.

SMS text codes are the weakest common MFA method: NIST restricts the use of the public telephone network (PSTN, which carries SMS and voice codes) as a restricted authenticator whose acceptance requires explicit risk acceptance and whose risks will likely increase over time; CISA states physical security tokens are the most secure form of MFA, followed by authenticator applications; Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant methods such as security keys over SMS.

MFA fatigue is an attack in which an attacker causes repeated authentication requests to be sent to a subscriber in an effort to get them to approve a fraudulent push-based request; NIST SP 800-63B rev. 4 defines this threat in its authentication-threat discussion. No method is perfect, and a prompt for a sign-in the user did not start should be treated as suspicious.

General defensive guidance: enable MFA on important accounts wherever it is offered (CISA: every user should sign up for MFA when available), and where a choice exists, prefer an authenticator app or a security key over text codes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How weak is SMS-based MFA, and is it worth using at all?
positions: Some vendor and popular coverage dismisses SMS MFA as effectively useless and says it should never be used.

NIST classifies the public telephone network (PSTN), which carries SMS and voice codes, as a restricted authenticator whose acceptance requires explicit risk acceptance and whose risks will likely increase over time.

CISA ranks physical security tokens as the most secure form of MFA, followed by authenticator applications, and Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant methods such as security keys over SMS-based sign-in; none of the three authorities suggests skipping MFA entirely when SMS is the only option.
CISA simultaneously calls MFA one of the most important cybersecurity practices and reports that enabling it makes account compromise up to 99 percent less likely.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the hierarchy (security keys strongest, authenticator apps next, SMS codes weakest) without dismissing SMS entirely: SMS-based MFA remains substantially better than no MFA, and the guidance is to prefer stronger methods when a choice exists.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's 'MFA is a foundational concept in Cybersecurity' framing and its toolbox-drawer analogy, which say nothing about authentication factors or proofs.
The draft's claim that MFA's value is that 'college courses use mfa as a building block' — a circular, content-free justification.
The draft's vocabulary entries (context, evidence, application) presented as if they define MFA.
The draft's quick-check items and worked example, which never mention passwords, factors, one-time codes, or attacks.
